subject: Lack of fit of pcount models

messages.author: b0084e74319ebcb3
messages.subject: Lack of fit of pcount models
parts:
Hello all,
I am evaluating how abundance is affected by vegetation structure variables in a bird species using replicated transects. For this I fitted several models using pcount and selected the best models using AIC. However, when performing a goodness of fit test I found a lack of fit for the top models (also, for most of the models I fitted). I think the problem might be with the size of the data set, because I already did this for other species with more data and did not have this problem. My question is: is it correct to make predictions based on this top models? Should I do something additional before obtaining these predictions? Any suggestion is very much appreciated. Thank you all in advance for your time and help.
Best,
Laura

parts:
Hello all,
Still thinking about this issue. Somebody advised me to try with occupancy models instead. I think in this case I prefer the N-mixture models implemented in pcount to take into account multiple detections during the same transect repetition (detecting one individual is different to detecting 4, and my data set had a lot of variation in this). However, I still tried fitting occupancy models and I am getting the same lack of fit problem. It is noteworthy that I am also running these analyses with other, more common, species and this has not been an issue. Therefore, I wanted to ask you all if you have advise on how to deal with the lack of fit in models. Moreover, if spite of the lack of fit it is possible to make predictions and biologically meaningful interpretations. Thank you all in advance for your time and help.
Best,
Laura

messages.author: 67eefb0e32c64fae
messages.subject: Re: Lack of fit of pcount models
parts:
Laura,

I encountered this issue myself a couple of weeks ago. You need to add a couple more steps (example code included):

1. Assess model fit for each candidate model using mb.gof.test()

fm2.gof <- mb.gof.test(fm2gof,print.table = TRUE,nsim = 1000,report = TRUE,plot.seasons = TRUE)

2. If any models are significantly (p < 0.05) under-dispersed (c-hat < 1), you don't need to do anything. Just make sure that c-hat in your original AIC is set to 1. If any models are significantly (p < 0.05) over-dispersed (c-hat > 1), you need to record their c-hat values and re-run the entire model set using Q-AIC. Run a separate Q-AIC analysis for each over-dispersed model, setting the Q-AIC c-hat value to that of the model you are focussing on.

QAICc1 <- aictab(cand.mods, second.ord = TRUE, nobs = NULL, sort = TRUE, c.hat = 2.73) #Over-dispersed model 1
QAICc2 <- aictab(cand.mods, second.ord = TRUE, nobs = NULL, sort = TRUE, c.hat = 2.78) #Over-dispersed model 2

3. Based on the QAIC values of the over-dispersed models, re-rank them within your original AIC analysis. They should have moved down a couple of ranks.

4. Remember that you now need to transform your parameter estimates of the over-dispersed models. For each over-dispersed model, multiply the standard errors of β (slope) and ρ (detection, or your parameter of interest) by √ ĉ.

5. You should now have some re-ranked models! Throw them into your AIC table, and just note that some have been ranked using QAIC.

Best,

Sean

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: Lack of fit of pcount models
parts:
Only detail I'd add is that instead of a call to mb.gof.test, maybe Nmix.gof.test instead, and that you shouldn't need to refit anything (rather, make post-hoc adjustments to SE and information criterion). I think there are several posts on the list that discuss what levels of over or underdispersion are annoying vs. seriously problematic, etc, but a few more recent efforts(e.g., here, here) might provide a little more insight into whether the fitted model produces really problematic estimates.

John

parts:
Hello all,

I wanted to give and update on this topic and ask your opinion again. Using Nmix.gof.test as suggested I found out that the problem was over dispersion, and this was an issue for all models, not only the top models. Therefore I obtained QAIC for all models in the data set and re-ranked them. I was surprised to find out that the ranking changed dramatically, and obtained different top models (including different variables to the top models based on AIC). My questions are:

1) Is this expected (radical differences in the ranking)? Should I just use the new ranking based on QAIC instead of the original? I am reluctant to do that because, although all models appear to have fit problems, over-dispersion in all cases appears to be mild (c-hat never higher than 1.6, usually around 1.3). However, I do think that adjustments of some kind are warranted because predictions from this models are not at all reasonable (too high).
2) About pos-hoc adjustments. Other than the SE, what other parameters should I adjust multiplying by c-hat? I did not fully understand what Sean refer to as my 'parameter of interest'. I mean, I want to obtain predictions of abundance (e.g. using predict), that would make it my parameter of interest? Or should I adjust detection?

I really appreciate your opinions and insights. Thank you all in advance for your time.

Best,

Laura

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: Lack of fit of pcount models
parts: 1) Is this expected (radical differences in the ranking)? Should I just use the new ranking based on QAIC instead of the original? I am reluctant to do that because, although all models appear to have fit problems, over-dispersion in all cases appears to be mild (c-hat never higher than 1.6, usually around 1.3). However, I do think that adjustments of some kind are warranted because predictions from this models are not at all reasonable (too high).

This isn't unexpected. AIC = -2 Log Like +2K; QAIC = 2 Log Like/c-hat +2K, so the contribution of the likelihood is being penalized. Larger sample size generally means a larger log-likelihood, so ranking differences between AIC and QAIC with c-hat held constant tend to be larger for larger sample sizes. I don't know of any justification for not making a correction for overdispersion.
2) About pos-hoc adjustments. Other than the SE, what other parameters should I adjust multiplying by c-hat?
It's suggested to adjust every standard error by sqrt(c-hat), but not the parameter estimates themselves.

messages.author: 1687709ed39768af
messages.subject: Re: Lack of fit of pcount models
parts:
Hi Laura,

This may be a late reply, but you should probably run your GoF test on your global model. Not your top ranking model or any other nested model. Any fit issues with your most complex model should extend to your simpler ones. Then use the c-hat you get from the goodness of fit on the global model to rank all of your models by QAIC and inflate your SEs of the parameter estimates. Or try a different distribution (ZIP or NB) and rerun the GoF on the global and see if the outcome improves.

Harrison
